title: Modi’s Great Anglo Paradox
gist: C. Raja Mohan argues that while Modi's BJP escalates a cultural decolonization campaign at home — purging English, renaming institutions, restyling army uniforms — the Indian state is simultaneously closing its deepest economic and political ties ever with the Anglosphere: the India-U.K. FTA entered force on July 15, 2026, a U.S. official says only 1 percent of work remains on an interim India-U.S. deal, and Canada and New Zealand agreements are queued. He frames the post-independence estrangement from the English-speaking world as a historical anomaly now being unwound, with the diaspora as the structural bridge.

insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan

insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: A Canada-India deal by year-end would complete the Anglosphere trade set; a date-stamped event to diary.

insights.claim: New Zealand signed a free trade agreement with New Delhi in April and Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has pushed for fast ratification, welcoming Modi personally at the airport on the first Indian premier's visit to New Zealand in 40 years.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Ratification pace is a readable proxy for how quickly small Anglosphere economies want Indian market access — dairy, agri and education flows.

insights.claim: India's trade diplomacy has been laser-focused on the West since it walked out of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership negotiations in 2019, following a failed decades-long quest for economic integration with China and Asia.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: India's supply-chain and trade gravity is tilting West, not intra-Asian — relevant to any China+1 sourcing thesis routed through India.

insights.claim: While India's foreign-policy community talks about multialignment, New Delhi's deepest and fastest-growing engagement today is with the Anglosphere — Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Discount the multialignment rhetoric when modelling Indian alignment risk; the revealed preference is Western.

insights.claim: Modi's decolonization campaign has moved past renaming roads and laws into reforming the armed forces, with the Indian Army issuing a new dress manual in June that strips residual colonial vestiges and introduces indigenous ceremonial dress such as the closed-neck bandi jacket.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Signals the nativist agenda is now reaching institutions with procurement budgets, not just symbols — watch domestic-content mandates.
insights.locator: The campaign has moved beyond renaming roads

insights.claim: Modi has pared back the government's use of English and actively promoted Hindi despite Gujarati being his own native language, and has increasingly replaced 'India' with 'Bharat' in official communication.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Language policy shifts affect education, media and services businesses that monetize English-medium demand in India.
insights.locator: In his Independence Day address from the Red Fort

insights.claim: Part of India's decolonization campaign is necessary modernization and part is pure political posturing, such as removing the bust of Edwin Lutyens — architect of imperial New Delhi — from the presidential palace, one of his own major works.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Distinguishing substance from symbolism keeps analysts from mistaking cultural noise for policy risk to foreign investors.
insights.locator: Part of the campaign is a necessary modernization

insights.claim: The BJP has inverted the postcolonial liberal script: where Manmohan Singh's Congress praised English and British institutions in a 2005 Oxford lecture while posturing against the West, the BJP rails against the colonial inheritance while expanding Western partnerships.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: The rhetoric-versus-policy inversion means Indian domestic nationalism is a poor predictor of India's external economic alignment.
insights.quote: The BJP has inverted the formula: As its decolonization agenda at home seeks to cut the remaining cultural ties, the government is growing the political and economic partnerships with the English-speaking world.
insights.locator: The BJP has inverted the formula

themes.theme: Diaspora and elites as the structural bridge

insights.claim: India's middle classes have voted with their feet toward the Anglosphere, which is the principal destination of their external engagement for study, work and settlement, and hosts the largest concentrations of overseas Indians outside the Persian Gulf.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Durable underpinning for education, remittance, travel and cross-border services flows regardless of who governs Delhi.
insights.quote: India’s middle classes have voted with their feet in their uninhibited embrace of the Anglo-Saxons
insights.locator: The BJP has inverted the formula

insights.claim: A recent British prime minister and U.S. vice president of Indian descent are merely reflections of a diaspora rise that also spans academia, media and business, and this diaspora undergirds the new commercial dynamic.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Diaspora penetration of Anglosphere elites is a structural tailwind for India-facing deal flow and policy access.
insights.locator: Undergirding the new commercial dynamic

insights.claim: Even the RSS, historically without international political networks, is now moving beyond activating the diaspora to cultivating local elites in the English-speaking world, with chief Mohan Bhagwat expected in the United States and Canada later this year.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Institutionalization of the Hindu right's Western outreach lowers the odds of an ideological reversal in India's Anglosphere tilt.

insights.claim: India's post-independence estrangement from the Anglo-Saxon powers was a historical anomaly born of specific context — messy decolonization and partition, the Anglo-U.S. tilt to Pakistan, and India's tilt to socialism and the Soviet Union — not a permanent structural divide.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: If the split was contingent rather than structural, the current convergence has far more room to run than consensus assumes.
insights.quote: the estrangement between India and the Anglo-Saxon powers was a historical anomaly born of a specific context

insights.claim: The 1991 economic reforms created the context for rediscovering long-suppressed economic and geopolitical synergies between India and the English-speaking world.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Places the current trade wave in a 35-year arc rather than treating it as a Modi-era policy fad.

insights.claim: Nehru's nonalignment did not prevent him from keeping India in the British Commonwealth, and the English-speaking Indian middle class remained a living bridge to the Anglosphere even at the height of the Cold War.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that Indian strategic autonomy rhetoric coexists comfortably with deep Western integration.

insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: The main tail risk to the India-Anglosphere trade trend is political, transmitted via diaspora disputes rather than economics.

insights.claim: On July 7 U.S. and Canadian authorities filed coordinated charges against several dozen members of India-based crime syndicates, including some tied to the 2023 assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar, underpinned by intelligence cooperation with Indian agencies and without alleging any Indian state role.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Removes the single biggest legal-diplomatic obstacle to a Canada-India deal — a concrete de-risking event for that negotiation.

insights.claim: Modi has stabilized the U.S. relationship through the turbulence of Trump's second term despite relentless accusations from opposition Congress leader Rahul Gandhi that he has surrendered to Trump.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Domestic political cost of the U.S. tilt is being absorbed, implying policy continuity rather than a pre-election reversal.

insights.claim: India cannot embrace the English-speaking world as a recipient of the latter's rules and conditions, so convergence must be built as a new bargain between sovereign equals rather than through Indian rule-taking.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Expect Indian negotiators to resist standards-and-conditionality clauses — a recurring sticking point in every pending FTA.
